blocks.text: And there the old Scholiast says: The poet wishes to show the size of the estates, how widely they extend in fields, so that not even kites can fly across them. This, then, suits the nature of the kite [col. 192] better: that it was called דאה daa from the excellence of its flight rather than ראה raa from its sight. You may object these words of Apuleius, Metamorphoses book 6: Yet I could not escape the kite's eyes of the crafty little old woman, in which remarkable keenness of sight seems to be attributed to the kite. I shall reply, 1. that the same is attributed to all birds of prey; 2. that this passage of Apuleius is unique. This the illustrious commentator Philippus Beroaldus acknowledges in these words: No writer, so far as I know, celebrates the eyes of the kite as excelling in keenness of sight. I add that in the Samaritan copy, both in Deuteronomy and in Leviticus, ࠃࠀࠄ is read with Daleth, nowhere ࠓࠀࠄ with Resh. And from the Hebrew דאה daa the Arabic حدا [ḥdā] hida seems to have been formed, with a guttural prefixed, as in the Hebrew name of the Tigris, חדקל Hiddekel, formed from the Chaldee דגלה Digla. At least this is certain: among the Arabs the kite is called حداة [ḥidāh] hida ^{(1)}. This is clear from Abenbitar, in the chapter قاطاننقي [qāṭānanqī] Catananke, in which these Greek words of Dioscorides on the dried seed of the herb catananke, Ἰκτίνου ὄνυξιν ὁμοιοῦται νεκροῦ [Iktinou onyxin homoioutai nekrou], It resembles the claws of a dead kite, are rendered thus in the Arabic paraphrase: وكان شكلها شبيها شكل مخالب الحداة الميتة [wa-kāna shakluhā shabīhan shakla makhālib al-ḥidāh al-mayyita] And its shape is similar to the shape of the claws of a dead hida. Hida, that is, kite. To say nothing of Damir, who in the chapter On حداة [ḥidāh] hida attributes to it whatever the Philosopher has about the kite, Hist. book 6, ch. 6. Nor of Andrea Bellunensis, whose words are: Alhada is a bird which is called the kite. Correct, except that alhida should be written, not alhada. For الحداة [al-ḥadāh] alhada with Fatha is a double axe, as Damir and Alcamus note; but alhida with Kasra is the name of the bird. There are some who interpret both דאה daa and ראה raa quite differently; but I pass over their versions because they do not seem in any way probable ^{(2)}.
